html:
This unit gives the designs for choosing a sample and the matching estimators, then the sampling distributions (z ,\ t ,\ \chi^{2}) used to make confidence statements. Every number below was recomputed by bca/tools/check_stats.py.

What this unit gives you
  • Simple random sampling with and without replacement; stratified, systematic, cluster, multistage and PPS sampling.
  • Ratio and regression estimation; estimating the population total and its variance.
  • Sampling distributions: z ,\ t and \chi^{2} with confidence intervals and tests.

6.1 Types of sampling

Probability sampling: simple random, stratified random, systematic, cluster, multistage, PPS. Non-probability: convenience, judgement (purposive), quota, snowball: no valid sampling-error estimate.

Notation: population size N, sample size n ,\ f = \frac{n}{N}, population mean Ȳ and variance S² = Σ(Yᵢ − Ȳ)²/(N − 1), sample mean ȳ and variance s^{2}.

6.2 Simple random sampling (SRS)

Every possible sample of size n has the same chance. Drawn without replacement (SRSWOR) by lottery or random numbers (a unit cannot appear twice) or with replacement (SRSWR) (a unit may repeat). Number of possible samples: C (N ,\ n) for SRSWOR, N^{n} for SRSWR.

SRSWOR SRSWR
Estimate of mean ȳ = \frac{\sum y}{n} (unbiased) ȳ
Variance of ȳ \frac{(1 - f) S^{2}}{n} \frac{\sigma^{2}}{n} = \frac{(N - 1) S^{2}}{N n}
Estimated \frac{(1 - f) s^{2}}{n} \frac{s^{2}}{n}
Estimate of total Y Ŷ = Nȳ Nȳ
Variance of total \frac{N^{2} (1 - f) s^{2}}{n} \frac{N^{2} s^{2}}{n}

(1 - f) is the finite population correction; sampling without replacement is more precise.

Worked example

A population of N = 200 students; an SRSWOR of n = 20 gives ȳ = 52 marks and s = 8. f = 0.1.

Estimated Var(ȳ) = (1 - 0.1) \times \frac{64}{20} = 2.88, SE = 1.697. 95% confidence interval for the mean: 52 \pm 1.96 \times 1.697 = (48.67, 55.33). Estimated total marks Ŷ = 200 \times 52 = 10,400, SE(Ŷ) = 200 \times 1.697 = 339.41.

With replacement the variance would be \frac{64}{20} = 3.2, larger than 2.88.

6.3 Stratified random sampling

Divide the population into non-overlapping, homogeneous strata (by district, class, income band), then draw an SRS in each. Estimate: ȳ_st = Σ W_h ȳ_h, W_{h} = \frac{N_{h}}{N}.

Var(ȳ_st) = Σ W_h² (1 − f_h) s_h²/n_h. It is more precise than SRS when strata are internally similar and differ from one another, guarantees representation of subgroups, and allows separate estimates per stratum.

Allocation of n: proportional n_{h} = \frac{n N_{h}}{N}; equal; optimum/Neyman n_{h} \propto N_{h} S_{h} (larger or more variable strata get more; with different costs ∝ \frac{N_{h} S_{h}}{\sqrt{c_{h}}}).

Worked example

Two strata: N₁ = 300 (ȳ₁ = 60, s₁ = 10), N₂ = 700 (ȳ₂ = 50, s₂ = 8); total n = 100, proportional allocation: n_{1} = 30 ,\ n_{2} = 70 ,\ W = 0.3 and 0.7. ȳ_st = 0.3 × 60 + 0.7 × 50 = 53. f_{1} = f_{2} = 0.1.

Var = 0.3^{2} \times 0.9 × 100/30 + 0.7^{2} \times 0.9 \times \frac{64}{70} = 0.27 + 0.4032 = 0.6732, SE = 0.8205. An SRS of the same 100 would have variance about 0.8622, so stratification cut the variance by 22%.

Neyman allocation: n_{1} \propto 300 \times 10 = 3000 ,\ n_{2} \propto 700 \times 8 = 5600 \to n_{1} = 100 × 3000/8600 = 34.9 \approx 35, n_{2} = 65.1 \approx 65.

6.4 Systematic sampling

Select every k-th unit after a random start: k = \frac{N}{n} (the sampling interval); choose a random start r from 1 \ldots k; the sample is r ,\ r + k ,\ r + 2 k ,\ \ldots.

Simple, spreads the sample evenly over an ordered list, no need for a full renumbering. Danger: if the list has a periodic pattern matching k (every 7th day of sales data) the sample is biased.

Equivalent to SRS if the list is in random order.

Worked example

N = 1,000, n = 50: k = 20. Random start 7 → units 7, 27, 47, 67, 87, …, 987. If N is not a multiple of n, use the nearest integer k or a circular list.

6.5 Cluster and multistage sampling

Cluster sampling: divide the population into clusters (villages, schools, wards), randomly select some clusters, and survey all units in them. Cheap and practical when no unit list exists and units are scattered.

Clusters are internally heterogeneous ideally; the higher the similarity within clusters (intra-cluster correlation) the less precise it is than SRS of the same size.

Multistage sampling samples in stages: districts → wards → households → persons; each stage uses SRS, systematic or PPS sampling.

It needs a list only for chosen units at each stage, and is the standard design for national surveys such as the Nepal Living Standards Survey and Demographic and Health Survey.

6.6 Probability proportional to size (PPS) sampling

When clusters differ in size, selecting each with probability proportional to its size removes the bias of giving small villages the same chance as big ones.

With p_{i} = \frac{M_{i}}{\sum M}, the unbiased Hansen–Hurwitz estimator for the total with n draws is Ŷ = \frac{\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) \sum y_{i}}{p_{i}}, and its variance is estimated from the spread of the \frac{y_{i}}{p_{i}} values.

Worked example

Three villages have 100, 300 and 600 households (total 1,000), so p = 0.1 ,\ 0.3 ,\ 0.6. Two draws select village 2 (y = 900 persons) and village 3 (y = 1,500). Ŷ = \frac{1}{2} ( 900 / 0.3 + 1,500/0.6) = \frac{1}{2} ( 3 ,\ 000 + 2,500) = 2,750 persons.

6.7 Ratio and regression methods of estimation

If an auxiliary variable x correlated with y is known for the whole population (total X, mean \bar{X}), it improves precision. Ratio estimator: R̂ = ȳ/x̄; ȳ_R = R̂ \bar{X}, Ŷ_R = R̂ X.

It is better than ȳ when y is roughly proportional to x (the line through the origin).

Regression estimator: ȳ_lr = ȳ + b (\bar{X} - \bar{x}), with b the sample regression coefficient of y on x; best when y is linearly related to x (with any intercept), and never worse than the ratio estimator in large samples. Both are slightly biased but precise.

Worked example

N = 100 farms with total area X = 5,000 h a (\bar{X} = 50). A sample of n = 10 gives mean production ȳ = 30 and mean area \bar{x} = 48. R̂ = \frac{30}{48} = 0.625.

Estimated mean production = 0.625 \times 50 = 31.25; total = 0.625 × 5,000 = 3,125. The raw ȳ = 30 would underestimate because the sample happened to have below-average farms (48 < 50); the ratio estimator corrects this.

Ratio and regression methods also apply within strata (separate or combined estimators). Estimating the population total and its variance: Ŷ = Nȳ under SRS; Ŷ_st = Σ N_h ȳ_h under stratification with Var(Ŷ_st) = Σ N_h²(1 − f_h)s_h²/n_h.

6.8 Sampling distributions: z, t and χ²

The sampling distribution of a statistic is its distribution over all possible samples. The central limit theorem: for large n the distribution of \bar{x} is approximately normal with mean μ and standard error \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, whatever the population shape.

Distribution When used Statistic
z (standard normal) mean, σ known or n large (\geq 30); proportions z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}}
Student's t mean, σ unknown, small n; df = n - 1 t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}
\chi^{2} (chi-square) tests of independence/goodness of fit; variance \chi^{2} = \frac{\sum (O - E)^{2}}{E}; df depends on the test

The t distribution is bell-shaped but heavier-tailed than z and approaches z as df grows.

Critical values (5% level): z = 1.645 (one-tail), 1.96 (two-tail), 2.576 (1% two-tail); t two-tail 0.05: df 9 \to 2.262 ,\ 14 \to 2.145 ,\ 15 \to 2.131 ,\ 19 \to 2.093 ;\ \chi^{2} at 5%: df 1 \to 3.841 ,\ 2 \to 5.991 ,\ 3 \to 7.815 ,\ 5 \to 11.070.

Worked example: confidence interval with t

A sample of n = 16 response times has mean 52.5 ms and s = 6. S E = \frac{6}{\sqrt{16}} = 1.5; df = 15, t₀.₀₂₅ = 2.1314. 95% C I = 52.5 \pm 2.1314 \times 1.5 = (49.30, 55.70) ms. Using z would give the narrower (49.56, 55.44), falsely overconfident for n = 16.

Worked example: z test

A system claims a mean load time of 50 s (\sigma = 10). A sample of n = 36 gives \bar{x} = 53. z = \frac{53 - 50}{\frac{10}{\sqrt{36}}} = 3 / 1.667 = 1.8. Two-tailed p-value = 0.0719 > 0.05, so we do not reject the claim at 5% (|z| < 1.96).

Worked example: χ² test of independence

Preference for a language by gender: 30 men and 20 women choose Java, and 20 men and 30 women choose Python, observed \begin{bmatrix} 30 & 20 \\ 20 & 30 \end{bmatrix}.

Totals are 50 per row and column, so each expected count is 25. \chi^{2} = \frac{\sum (O - E)^{2}}{E} = 4 \times \frac{25}{25} = 4.0, df = (2 - 1) (2 - 1) = 1; critical value 3.841 ;\ p = 0.0455 → reject independence at 5%: preference appears related to gender in this sample.

Goodness of fit: a die rolled 60 times gives counts 8, 12, 9, 11, 10, 10; expected 10 each; \chi^{2} = \frac{4 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0}{10} = 1.0 < 11.07 (df 5): consistent with a fair die.

6.9 Pictures of sampling designs and sampling distributions

6.10 Eight sampling designs and tools, and what each is used for

  1. Simple random sampling. Every unit has the same chance, like drawing lots, so the estimate is unbiased and easy to analyse. It suits a small, well-listed population such as 200 students of one batch. It is the baseline against which other designs are compared.
  2. Stratified sampling. The population is split into alike groups (strata) such as Terai, hill and mountain, and each is sampled separately. This guarantees that every group is represented and often gives a smaller variance than simple random sampling. A national household survey in Nepal is naturally stratified by ecological region.
  3. Systematic sampling. Pick a random start and then every k-th unit, such as every 20th voter on a list. It is quick, spreads the sample evenly and needs no random-number table. It fails if the list repeats with the same period as k, for example a weekly pattern with k = 7.
  4. Cluster and multistage sampling. Whole villages, wards or schools are chosen at random and then units inside them are surveyed. It cuts travel cost enormously when no list of individuals exists. The price is a larger error, because people in one ward resemble each other.
  5. PPS sampling. Big clusters are given a bigger chance of selection, in proportion to size. A village with 600 households is then six times more likely to be drawn than one with 100. The estimator divides each total by its selection probability to stay unbiased.
  6. Ratio and regression estimation. When an easy-to-know variable such as farm area is correlated with the target, say production, it sharpens the estimate. The ratio estimator uses the known population total of the helper variable. It gave 31.25 instead of 30 in the worked example of Section 6.7.
  7. The z and t distributions. They give confidence intervals and tests for a mean. Use z when σ is known or n is large, and t when σ is unknown and n is small, as Gosset showed. A software tester comparing the load times of 12 pages uses t.
  8. The chi-square test. It compares observed counts with expected counts. A college can test whether language preference differs by gender, or whether a die or random-number generator is fair. The decision rule is the shaded tail of Figure 6.3.

6.11 Hypothesis testing in full: errors, power and the standard tests

Section 6.8 gave the tools. A complete test follows the same six steps every time.

  1. State the null hypothesis H_0 (no effect, no difference) and the alternative H_1 (one-tailed or two-tailed).
  2. Fix the significance level \alpha (usually 0.05), the probability of rejecting H_0 when it is true.
  3. Choose the test statistic (z, t, \chi^2 or F) from the data type, sample size and what is known.
  4. Compute the statistic and either compare it with the critical value or find the p-value.
  5. Decide: reject H_0 if |\text{statistic}| exceeds the critical value, equivalently if p < \alpha.
  6. Write the conclusion in words about the problem. "Do not reject" means the evidence is insufficient, not that H_0 is proved.

Two kinds of error. A Type I error is rejecting a true H_0; its probability is \alpha. A Type II error is failing to reject a false H_0; its probability is \beta. The power of a test is 1 - \beta, the chance of detecting a real effect.

For a fixed sample size, lowering \alpha raises \beta; the only way to lower both is to take a larger sample.

Decision H_0 true H_0 false
Reject H_0 Type I error (probability \alpha) Correct (power 1 - \beta)
Do not reject H_0 Correct (1 - \alpha) Type II error (probability \beta)
Worked example: Type II error and power

H_0: \mu = 50 against H_1: \mu > 50 with \sigma = 10, n = 36, so \mathrm{SE} = \frac{10}{6} = 1.667 and \alpha = 0.05. Reject if \bar{x} > 50 + 1.645(1.667) = 52.74. Suppose the true mean is really 54.

The test fails to reject when \bar{x} \leq 52.74, which has probability \beta = P\!\left(Z \leq \frac{52.74 - 54}{1.667}\right) = P(Z \leq -0.76) = 0.225, so the power is 0.775.

With a two-tailed test at the same \alpha the acceptance region is 46.73 to 53.27 and the power for a true mean of 54 falls to 0.670: a one-tailed test is more powerful in the direction it looks.

The standard tests at a glance.

Situation Statistic Degrees of freedom
One mean, \sigma unknown t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} n - 1
Two independent means, equal variances t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}}, s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2} n_1 + n_2 - 2
Paired measurements t = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} on the differences n - 1
Two variances F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2} (larger on top) n_1 - 1,\ n_2 - 1
One proportion z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0 q_0/n}} none (normal)
Worked example: one-sample t

Claim: the mean response time is 50 ms. A sample of n = 16 gives \bar{x} = 54 and s = 6. t = \frac{54 - 50}{6/4} = \frac{4}{1.5} = 2.667 with 15 d.f. The two-tailed critical value is 2.131 and p = 0.0176, so reject the claim at 5%: the true mean is probably higher.

Worked example: two independent samples

Two sorting routines are timed: A on 10 runs with mean 72 and s = 6, B on 12 runs with mean 66 and s = 7. s_p^2 = \frac{9(36) + 11(49)}{20} = 43.15, \mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{43.15\left(\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{12}\right)} = 2.813, t = \frac{6}{2.813} = 2.13 with 20 d.f.

The critical value is 2.086 and p = 0.0455, so reject equal means at 5%. A 95% confidence interval for the difference is 6 \pm 2.086(2.813) = (0.13, 11.87), which just excludes 0, in agreement with the test.

The F check of the equal-variance assumption: F = \frac{49}{36} = 1.36 against the 5% critical value 3.10 (11, 9 d.f.), so the variances are not significantly different and pooling is acceptable.

Worked example: paired t and a proportion

Paired. Page-load times (s) of 8 devices before and after an optimisation: before 12, 15, 11, 14, 13, 16, 12, 15; after 10, 13, 11, 11, 12, 13, 10, 14.

The differences are 2, 2, 0, 3, 1, 3, 2, 1: \bar{d} = 1.75, s_d = 1.035, t = \frac{1.75}{1.035/\sqrt{8}} = 4.78 with 7 d.f. (critical 2.365, p = 0.002): the optimisation is effective.

Treating the two columns as independent samples would waste the pairing and give a much weaker test.

Proportion. In a survey of 200 users 118 prefer the new interface. H_0: p = 0.5. \hat{p} = 0.59 and z = \frac{0.59 - 0.5}{\sqrt{0.25/200}} = 2.55, p = 0.011: reject, a majority prefers it.

A 95% interval is 0.59 \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.59 \times 0.41}{200}} = (0.522, 0.658).

Formula and fact sheet

  • SRSWOR: Var(ȳ) = \frac{(1 - f) s^{2}}{n}; total Ŷ = Nȳ, Var = \frac{N^{2} (1 - f) s^{2}}{n}. SRSWR: \frac{s^{2}}{n}.
  • Stratified: ȳ_st = ΣW_hȳ_h; Var = \frac{\sum W_{h}^{2} (1 - f_{h}) s_{h}^{2}}{n_{h}}; Neyman n_{h} \propto N_{h} S_{h}.
  • Systematic: k = \frac{N}{n}, random start. PPS: Ŷ = \frac{\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) \sum y_{i}}{p_{i}}. Ratio: ȳ_R = (ȳ/x̄)X̄.
  • SE of mean \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} ;\ z = 1.96 (95%); t with df n - 1 ;\ \chi^{2} = \frac{\sum (O - E)^{2}}{E}, df = (r - 1) (c - 1).
  • Errors: \alpha = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ true}), \beta = P(\text{keep } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ false}), power = 1 - \beta.
  • Pooled s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}; paired t = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d/\sqrt{n}}; F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}; proportion z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0 q_0/n}}.

Chapter summary

  • SRS is the baseline; stratification gains precision from homogeneous strata; systematic sampling is simple but pattern-sensitive; cluster and multistage designs cut cost; PPS handles unequal clusters.
  • Ratio and regression estimators exploit an auxiliary variable.
  • The CLT justifies z ;\ t replaces z for small n with unknown \sigma ;\ \chi^{2} tests counts.
  • A complete hypothesis test states H_0 and H_1, fixes \alpha, computes a statistic and concludes in words; Type I and II errors trade off, and power rises with sample size; paired, two-sample, variance and proportion tests extend the one-sample tests.

Model answers: medium (5 marks) and long (10 marks) questions

Q1 (5 marks). A population has N = 800 students. A simple random sample without replacement of n = 40 gives mean marks ȳ = 65 and s = 10. Estimate the variance and standard error of the mean, a 95% confidence interval, and the population total with its standard error.

Introduction. Under SRSWOR the sample mean is an unbiased estimate of the population mean and its variance includes the finite population correction (1 - f), where f = \frac{n}{N}.

Sampling fraction. f = 40/800 = 0.05, so 1 - f = 0.95.

Variance and SE. Est. Var(ȳ) = \frac{(1 - f) s^{2}}{n} = 0.95 × 100/40 = 2.375, so SE(ȳ) = \sqrt{2.375} = 1.541.

Confidence interval. ȳ ± 1.96 S E = 65 \pm 1.96 \times 1.541 = 65 \pm 3.02, that is (61.98, 68.02).

Total. Ŷ = Nȳ = 800 \times 65 = 52,000. SE(Ŷ) = N × SE(ȳ) = 800 \times 1.541 = 1,232.9.

Interpretation and conclusion. We are 95% confident the true mean mark lies between about 62 and 68. Without the correction the SE would be 1.581, a little too large, so ignoring (1 - f) overstates the uncertainty.

The estimates are valid only if the 40 students were truly chosen at random from a complete list (Figure 6.1a).

Q2 (5 marks). A population has two strata: N_{1} = 600 with s_{1} = 4 and N_{2} = 400 with s_{2} = 12. Allocate a sample of n = 50 by (a) proportional and (b) Neyman allocation, and compare the variances.

Introduction. Stratified sampling draws a separate random sample from each stratum. The allocation decides how many units come from each.

\ast (a) Proportional allocation n_{h} = \frac{n N_{h}}{N}. n_{1} = 50 × 600/1000 = 30 and n_{2} = 50 × 400/1000 = 20*.

\ast (b) Neyman (optimum) allocation n_{h} \propto N_{h} S_{h}. N_{1} S_{1} = 2,400 and N_{2} S_{2} = 4,800, total 7,200. n_{1} = 50 × 2400/7200 = 16.7 ≈ 17; n_{2} = 50 × 4800/7200 = 33.3 ≈ 33*.

Variance of the stratified mean Var = \frac{\sum W_{h}^{2} (1 - f_{h}) s_{h}^{2}}{n_{h}} with W_{1} = 0.6 and W_{2} = 0.4.

Allocation n_{1} ,\ n_{2} Var(ȳ_st) SE
Proportional 30, 20 1.2768 1.130
Neyman 17, 33 0.9698 0.985

Conclusion. Neyman allocation gives a 24% smaller variance because it samples more heavily from the highly variable stratum 2. It is the best design when the strata differ strongly in variability; proportional allocation is simpler and nearly as good when they do not.

Q3 (10 marks). Explain the z ,\ t and chi-square distributions with their uses. A sample of 9 response times has mean 52 ms and s = 6 ms. Test H_{0}: \mu = 48 ms against H_{1}: \mu \neq 48 ms at the 5% level and give a 95% confidence interval. Compare with a z-test.

Introduction. The sampling distribution of a statistic is its distribution over all possible samples.

By the central limit theorem the sample mean is approximately normal with standard error \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} for large n (Figure 6.2). Three families are used for inference.

The three distributions (Table).

Distribution Use Statistic Shape
z (standard normal) mean with known σ or n \geq 30; proportions z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}} symmetric bell
Student's t mean, σ unknown, small n; df = n - 1 t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}} symmetric, heavier tails
\chi^{2} goodness of fit, independence, variance \chi^{2} = \frac{\sum (O - E)^{2}}{E} skewed right, df-dependent

Key points. The t curve approaches the normal as df grows (Plate 6.1 ) ;\ \chi^{2} is never negative and its decision tail is on the right (Figure 6.3).

Hypothesis test (t-test).

  1. Hypotheses: H_{0}: \mu = 48 ;\ H_{1}: \mu \neq 48 (two-tailed).
  2. Statistic: S E = \frac{6}{\sqrt{9}} = 2. t = \frac{52 - 48}{2} = 2.0, with df = 8.
  3. Critical value: t₀.₀₂₅ with 8 df = 2.306.
  4. Decision: |2.0| < 2.306, so we do not reject H_{0}. The two-tailed p-value is 0.0805, greater than 0.05.

Confidence interval. 52 \pm 2.306 \times 2 = 52 \pm 4.61, that is (47.39, 56.61). The value 48 lies inside, which agrees with the test.

Comparison with z . \ast If σ were wrongly taken as 6 (known), z = 2.0 and the critical value is 1.96, so the same data would reject H_{0} (p = 0.0455). The z-test is too eager with only 9 observations because it ignores the extra uncertainty of estimating σ; that is exactly why Gosset invented the t* distribution.

Conclusion. With a small sample and unknown σ, use t. Here the evidence (52 ms against 48 ms) is suggestive but not statistically significant at the 5% level; a larger sample would be needed to settle it.
